title: Eno Reyes - Building the Software Factory

segments.text: ENO REYES: Hey, everybody.
I'm excited to chat today about-- oh, is it this thing?
Oh yeah.
Great.
Excited to chat today about this concept of the software factory
and a little bit about what we're doing.
And so when I talk about the software factory,
I always like to reflect on how insanely quick
this entire field has actually evolved.
Three and a half years ago, basically--
we started three and a half years ago.
And back then, autocomplete was basically
the only known workflow for introducing
AI into, at least, DevTools that were-- let's just, say what
we now consider to be standard, like agentic or semi-agentic,
LLM-based workflows.
And so autocomplete moved on to chatbots.
Chatbots moved on to agents.
And agents are now moving into software factories.
So what does that actually mean?
Well, if the slides were ordered well, that I had sent-- my bad--
I would be talking about exactly this, which
is that a software factory is really
this process where signals flow into your system,
or your business.
These signals could take a lot of different forms.
But traditionally, if you're building,
let's say, a piece of software that helps people
manage information, or you're a school system
and you're trying to build some software for that,
maybe you're a financial services firm
and you're doing a bunch of stuff to manage transactions,
the signals that you're ingesting
might be things like customer feedback, internal data,
telemetry, an executive saying, we're going to pivot.
It could be a lot of different things.
And all of these signals today, human beings
actually triage themselves in their heads.
And it's almost never explicitly represented in any real system.
At that point, those signals are then ingested.
And luckily, if you're operating on signals
for things like a bug or an error,
you hopefully have telemetry for that.
But ultimately, that triage process
is very human-driven today in almost all organizations.
Then you go and you start to plan.
And really, that's the first time
that you start to encode any of this information anywhere.
You'll typically do this in something like Jira,
or maybe Notion.
Maybe you're doing it in Confluence.
But either way, this planning process
tends to be fairly unstructured at most organizations.
And then you start to move into actually writing the code,
validating the code, shipping, deploying.
And ultimately, with deployed, monitored software,
it starts to generate more signals.
So what's interesting is this implicit feedback loop
exists at almost every company building software.
And yet an explicit model of this
does not really exist anywhere.
And so what we've found is that-- what's interesting
about this is that if you think about the hard part
of this problem, coding is just not the hard part.
It's basically, in fact, the easiest part of this problem.
And in fact, all of the other things around actually writing
code are the hard part, the part that leads to mess.
And I think that when a lot of people
think about the velocity aspect of-- you have an AI CEO saying,
oh, AGI is here.
It's like six months away.
You're going to see 100x productivity.
And then you yourself have not seen that at your company.
A lot of people are asking the question, why is that?
Well, really, it's because you're actually only AI-ifying
one narrow slice of this process.
And then a lot of it remains a very human-driven,
synchronous workflow, where you go
and you say to a machine something that basically
looks like autocomplete.
I want the thing.
You give it back to me, I send you on a task.
It comes back to me.
And so what we want to do is we want to say, how do we basically
design a system that allows signals
to flow all the way to deployed software
without human intervention?
And so when I say without human intervention,
I don't mean without humans at all being
involved in the process.
And that leads to a lot of the questions that I think people
are asking right now-- which are probably very hard to read
on this slide--
things like, how do we prevent cost overruns
if this fully autonomous system is operating without impunity?
How do we ensure we have access to the best possible AI systems
regardless of who wins the model race, who wins the AI layer
race?
You've already heard-- I think that last one did
a good job of showing how much complexity there
is in the vendor ecosystem.
You don't really want to be making a bet
on any one of these things.
You just want to be building a system.
So how do you do that?
Also, how does the role of the human evolve in this new system?
If you're not intervening as the signal flows
all the way to deployed software, what are you doing?
And then how does that change the organization?
I think that, generally, you should then
be thinking, well, OK, if I'm not doing that, then I'm clearly
somehow involved in building this system
or maintaining, refining, or evolving the software factory.
And that is ultimately the new role for people.
And so if you're thinking about, what
does it mean for me to build, refine, or evolve
a software factory?
You should be thinking about a couple of things,
of, one, how should this system be designed?
Well, we have a couple of opinions.
The first is that you should be model-independent.
If you are operating in a world where
you're going to delegate your software
factory to a single model vendor,
and they're going to make a ton of arguments that are actually
not that compelling, but maybe they'll
make compelling arguments that, oh, you have to verticalize
aggressively, and your agent harness needs
to be with the model, we found, empirically,
that's very clearly not true.
You actually want to aggregate and commoditize
that model layer in order for you
to have access to the true Pareto frontier of both cost
and quality, all right?
And so then the second thing is, who should own this?
Well, we literally make SaaS to help you build this,
but I still think that you should be in control
of whatever software you use.
And so we also offer things like on-prem,
air-gapped, all the way to basically you sign a contract
and we throw it over and we don't see it again.
And that is because we believe you
should be the sovereign of your software factory.
It's incredibly important that your software factory operates
regardless of what vendors come and go,
because, ultimately, your software
factory is your company.
If you build software, you're basically
describing the new version of your business.
And so it's really important that you're
able to maintain and control that.
And then the last is you should really
be thinking about your software factory
as something that operates across every action that
takes place inside of your product and engineering
organization.
So if there is basically any activity,
any context, any workflow, that's
a part of your software factory.
And there's a lot of stuff that you
can do, everything from code review,
to security analysis, to testing documentation, incident
response.
But at the end of the day, each of these workflows
should probably operate with, effectively,
a shared agent core, because--
I think that there was actually--
I really enjoyed the talk just a bit ago
that was talking about this idea of,
if you have a ton of different specialized agents,
like a code review agent and an incident response agent,
you end up in this weird microservice system
where you're hyperoptimizing each of those agent
architectures for what is ultimately one shared
workflow, which is gathering information, acting
on information on computer systems,
and informing the user as it does that.
And so you really want this singular AI agent system
where the context and the workflow changes.
Code review is obviously a very different workflow
from incident response.
But ultimately, it's actually, at a high level,
all just going to be like computer control
on top of the agent with context.
So using a shared agent core to then operate
across many surfaces that your software factory may touch
is also super important.
And in a larger organization, you're
probably thinking about things like governance.
How do we handle consistency?
How do we handle ensuring that an agent doesn't go and drop
a bunch of tables?
What about IT ops?
A bunch of stuff like this becomes very clear.
I would argue that this is ultimately
the responsibility of whatever agent platform you're using,
to enforce all of these standardized controls.
And you really should be asking, is there a page called
enterprise controls or organizational controls?
And how many are there?
And if you're not seeing hundreds of different scenarios
that a agent platform has gone through in order to basically
refine preventing bad things from happening with agents,
then I would just start looking out and see what is out there.
There's open-source standards.
Docker just came out with a really interesting 35-control
system for this, where they said,
what are the agent controls that you need inside of an agent
platform?
Sort of vendor-neutral?
I thought that was a pretty cool way of delivering that.
And so then that leads you to this next interesting point,
which is that, almost certainly, after all this work of talking
about agents, you've actually maybe not fixed
the biggest problem that's preventing agents
from succeeding, which is the state of your environment.
And so I always like to draw the analogy of human beings.
200,000 years ago, we're not that different.
We're pretty much the same humans, more or less,
but we're so much more advanced.
What happened?
Well, we completely changed our environment around us.
And so, yes, you can wait for agents
to continue to get better.
They will probably continue to get better.
But I think that really updating the code
base and the engineering system around your software factory
is, by far, the highest leverage changes that you can make.
And really, that's looking at things like dev reproducibility,
environment cleanliness linting
type checking, quality tests.
Really, the actual tidbit would be, what is the amount of--
or do you have enough deterministic,
verifiable feedback loops inside of your organization
to give agents the ability to succeed without needing
to consult a human?
So it's one thing if you wait for code review to say,
that code is not organized well.
It's much better to have a deterministic signal that says,
that code is not organized well.
And agents can then use that to loop and validate
their work until they succeed.
So, yeah, here's a laundry list of controls that matter.
Security, governance, and enablement, all of these
are super important.
I don't want to blaze through this,
but I think it's like the type of thing
where you can take a photo.
Ultimately, my view is that your agents
are going to have to have access ultimately in the software
factory that is dangerous.
It's just how it's going to happen.
It's not really a matter of if, but just when.
And so you have to treat them the way that you would
human beings, which is you build out systems of control,
and you build out layers.
So how do you prevent a human from dropping an important table
in your company?
Well, you may be relying today on basically telling them not
to do that.
That is actually not good.
And probably the analogy that-- if you've ever
thought about building software organizations for more
than, say, 50 to 75 people, you start to realize that even
50 to 75 incredibly competent people, someone's
going to eventually drop the database.
And so you really have to think about introducing these agents
as scaling up the guardrails, prevention, et cetera,
towards what an organization maybe 10 times larger
than your current organization would look
like-- which is interesting.
Because if you're a five-person startup,
that means you're actually operating the controls that
maybe a 50-person company would need.
If you're a 50-person company, 500 people.
And so you really have to up-level
a lot of the guardrails and the systems
that are actually very well-established.
And I think you don't really need to reinvent the wheel here.
You should look at software development best practices
and then just ensure that they're
being enforced on those agents.
And so on that idea, I think that this is probably
the most interesting and evolving part of humans' roles
in the software factory.
I sort of alluded to this earlier,
but we've already just labeled a bunch of things that I'm
suggesting that you change.
This is what we're going to do.
We're going to say, what are the guardrails that exist?
Oh, there aren't guardrails for that.
Let's actually implement the guardrails for that.
We're going to look at where agents are failing.
And what are we going to do?
We're going to add context.
We're going to update the workflows
that the agents are following.
Actually, if you listen to any talks--
and I highly recommend listening to talk
about chip fabricators or any of these really advanced, industry
4.0, actual real life factories--
you start to realize there's whole dedicated roles of process
control, process management, loop management of people
who basically just look and say, OK, great.
We lost 10% of the resources due to this bad inefficiency.
Let's go fix that part of the factory,
and then we're going to reiterate and refine.
We're basically going to be doing that for software systems.
And so I think a lot about this process of,
how do you observe failures in your software factory?
How do you intervene when you are
seeing either, one, a one-off, or two, a consistent failure?
And three, how do you then refine iteratively
those workflows?
It ends up as everything does, boiling down
to evals and verifiability.
How do you evaluate whether or not a failure happened?
The case study here would be code review.
Pretty much everyone in here who's
thinking about a software factory, the first step you
can make is building a system that
makes you confident to merge maybe 5%, then 10%, then 50%,
then 100% of your PRs without human code review.
What would that look like?
What is that system?
And that doesn't mean that you still
don't need humans to understand the code changes.
That's a separate part.
But ultimately, you probably need something like what
self-driving cars had, which was--
this is kind of dark, but fatalities on the road.
Everyone knows, when the fatalities on the road
drops below--
the order of magnitude is what's interesting.
Maybe it's the same as humans.
Maybe it's 10 times less than humans.
But there's some sort of metric where we go, great.
We think this is safer than the human,
so we're happy to let this thing start driving.
Similarly, with validation, you need to get to the point
where you say, what are my metrics that I'm
going to measure to allow that review step to happen
without a human in the loop?
And maybe you feel that it's bugs.
Maybe it's incident responses--
or sorry, incidents.
Maybe it's MTTR.
Maybe you want to look at a bunch of these things
together and say, we think that maybe our system is now
safer than humans being involved,
so we're going to let that thing run.
And you should probably have engineers thinking
about that inside your company.
I sort of just alluded to this as well,
which is, what are the outcomes then that you're measuring?
I would be looking at cycle time.
I'd be looking at code shelf life, incident time, number
of bugs that have occurred.
Do not measure tokens.
It really does not give you a ton of information or value.
And so you can also look at costs in other ways, maybe just
cost per code change, cost per loop
or per week, almost treating it in a way
that we do humans with salary.
And those are the things that you can then measure and iterate
and optimize against.
So if you take three things away,
it would be, one, invest in agent-readiness.
That is super important.
We build a product for that, which is pretty cool.
Two, govern before you scale.
You want to implement all this stuff
before you start immediately rolling this out
across the whole company.
And three, you've got to be thinking about the outcomes
that you want to measure in advance, because--
I think the last deck just had this--
you can't optimize against something that you
aren't measuring.
So really important to have all this stuff together.
And hopefully, this was helpful in thinking about building
your software factories.
Thank you.
